summary: "Android throttles gyroscopes to 200 Hz to stop motion sensors acting as microphones — but Camera2 pipelines leak 800–1000 Hz gyroscope data through vendor metadata, and a zero-profiling attack transcribes 52% of spoken words."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-23-camera-can-hear-you-acoustic-side-channel.svg"
---

Android has a defence against phones that double as microphones: since Android 12, `SensorManager` caps gyroscope and accelerometer rates at **200 Hz**, demands a special permission for anything faster, and throttles sensors back down whenever the microphone toggle is switched off. The idea is that you cannot reconstruct speech from a 200 Hz motion trace, because voice energy sits far above that band.

**Camera2 quietly routes around it.** During an active camera session, the Camera HAL stabilisation pipeline records high-rate gyroscope measurements and exports them through vendor-specific `CaptureResult` metadata. Loudspeaker speech shakes the chassis, and those vibrations couple straight into the stabilisation path. The metadata channel therefore carries a high-rate motion trace while the system-wide rate limit stays intact.

The measurement is broad and uncomfortable. Across **50 smartphones from 10 vendors** (2020–2026), 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and **26 exceed 200 Hz** — including six flagship models running at 800–1000 Hz, double what `SensorManager` permits. The channel needs neither `RECORD_AUDIO` nor `HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS`. It also survives the privacy switches: turning the microphone off does not throttle the metadata, and turning the camera off blanks only the video frames while the 800–1000 Hz stream keeps going.

The attack itself is the second contribution. Prior microphone-equivalent attacks train on real sensor traces, which entangles the speech content with one phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate — so they do not transfer to a phone you have never touched. **Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L)** decouples the two by training a recogniser on a physics-constrained forward simulator instead of real device data. The resulting universal recogniser, **CamEar**, reaches **52.1% mean word accuracy** (up to 61.8%) and **74.3% character accuracy** on the six 800–1000 Hz phones. By comparison, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data fall to **25.9%** word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and beats ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.

Caveats: 52% word accuracy is far from a reliable transcript, the leakage path is vendor-dependent (only 37 of 50 devices expose it), and the paper does not describe a fix on the OS side. But the policy question is the sharp part — a permission model that assumes motion data is low-rate is simply wrong once the camera is on.

Source: [arXiv:2611.27964 — Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27964)
